claim: Rad51 is the key protein in homologous recombination (HR), a major DNA double-strand break repair pathway.
source: Although Rad51 is the key protein in homologous recombination (HR), a major DNA double-strand break repair pathway, several auxiliary factors interact with Rad51 to promote productive HR.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about Rad51's role in HR.

claim: Several auxiliary factors interact with Rad51 to promote productive HR.
source: Although Rad51 is the key protein in homologous recombination (HR), a major DNA double-strand break repair pathway, several auxiliary factors interact with Rad51 to promote productive HR.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: Two distinct sites within the intrinsically disordered N-terminus of Sfr1 (Sfr1N) cooperatively bind Rad51.
source: Two distinct sites within the intrinsically disordered N-terminus of Sfr1 (Sfr1N) were found to cooperatively bind Rad51.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 2-4.

claim: Deletion of the Sfr1N domain impaired Rad51 stimulation in vitro.
source: Deletion of this domain impaired Rad51 stimulation in vitro and rendered cells sensitive to DNA damage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Deletion of the Sfr1N domain rendered cells sensitive to DNA damage.
source: Deletion of this domain impaired Rad51 stimulation in vitro and rendered cells sensitive to DNA damage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Amino acid-substitution mutants of Sfr1N had comparable biochemical defects to the deletion mutant.
source: By contrast, amino acid-substitution mutants, which had comparable biochemical defects, could promote DNA repair, suggesting that Sfr1N has another role in addition to Rad51 binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Amino acid-substitution mutants of Sfr1N could promote DNA repair despite having biochemical defects.
source: By contrast, amino acid-substitution mutants, which had comparable biochemical defects, could promote DNA repair, suggesting that Sfr1N has another role in addition to Rad51 binding.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7A.

claim: Sfr1N has another role in addition to Rad51 binding.
source: By contrast, amino acid-substitution mutants, which had comparable biochemical defects, could promote DNA repair, suggesting that Sfr1N has another role in addition to Rad51 binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutants with impaired Rad51 binding can still promote DNA repair.

claim: DNA repair observed in Sfr1N amino acid-substitution mutants was dependent on Rad55-Rad57.
source: Unexpectedly, the DNA repair observed in these mutants was dependent on Rad55-Rad57, another auxiliary factor complex hitherto thought to function independently of Swi5-Sfr1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Rad55-Rad57 was previously thought to function independently of Swi5-Sfr1.
source: Unexpectedly, the DNA repair observed in these mutants was dependent on Rad55-Rad57, another auxiliary factor complex hitherto thought to function independently of Swi5-Sfr1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genetic studies (Akamatsu et al., 2003; Akamatsu et al., 2007).

claim: Swi5-Sfr1 and Rad55-Rad57 form a higher-order complex.
source: When combined with the finding that they form a higher-order complex, our results imply that Swi5-Sfr1 and Rad55-Rad57 can collaboratively stimulate Rad51 in Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7E,F.

claim: Swi5-Sfr1 and Rad55-Rad57 can collaboratively stimulate Rad51 in Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
source: When combined with the finding that they form a higher-order complex, our results imply that Swi5-Sfr1 and Rad55-Rad57 can collaboratively stimulate Rad51 in Schizosaccharomyces pombe.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of biochemical and genetic data presented in Figure 7.

claim: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are a particularly toxic form of DNA damage in which a DNA molecule is broken into two (or more) fragments.
source: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are a particularly toxic form of DNA damage in which a DNA molecule is broken into two (or more) fragments.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DSBs.

claim: Homologous recombination (HR) is a major DSB repair pathway.
source: A major DSB repair pathway is homologous recombination (HR).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about HR.

claim: During HR, an intact stretch of DNA that shares sequence similarity to the DSB site is identified and utilized as a template for synthesis-dependent repair.
source: During HR, an intact stretch of DNA that shares sequence similarity to the DSB site is identified and utilized as a template for synthesis-dependent repair.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the HR mechanism.

claim: Dysregulation of HR results in misrepair of DSBs, resulting in genomic instability, a potent driver of tumorigenesis.
source: Dysregulation of HR results in misrepair of DSBs, resulting in genomic instability, a potent driver of tumorigenesis (Jeggo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jeggo et al., 2016.

claim: HR is initiated by the formation of 3' single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) at the DSB site.
source: HR is initiated by the formation of 3' single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) at the DSB site.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about HR initiation.

claim: The ssDNA at the DSB site is first bound by RPA, then by Rad51.
source: This ssDNA is first bound by RPA, then by the ubiquitous RecA-family recombinase Rad51, which forms a right-handed nucleoprotein filament.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the order of protein binding during HR.

claim: Rad51 forms a right-handed nucleoprotein filament on ssDNA.
source: This ssDNA is first bound by RPA, then by the ubiquitous RecA-family recombinase Rad51, which forms a right-handed nucleoprotein filament.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Rad51 filament structure.

claim: The Rad51 filament is able to capture intact double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) and identify regions of DNA that share substantial sequence similarity to the DSB site.
source: The Rad51 filament is able to capture intact double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) and—by assessing the extent of base-pairing with the filamentous ssDNA—identify regions of DNA that share substantial sequence similarity to the DSB site (Prentiss et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prentiss et al., 2015.

claim: After initial pairing with the complementary strand of the dsDNA, the Rad51 filament displaces the noncomplementary strand by driving strand transfer, resulting in the formation of a displacement loop.
source: After initial pairing with the complementary strand of the dsDNA, the Rad51 filament further displaces the noncomplementary strand by driving strand transfer, resulting in the formation of an intermediate structure known as a displacement loop.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the strand exchange mechanism.

claim: The 3' end of the invading strand is utilized as a primer for DNA synthesis, leading to its extension and the recovery of lost genetic information.
source: The 3' end of the invading strand is then utilized as a primer for DNA synthesis, leading to its extension and the recovery of lost genetic information.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DNA synthesis during HR.

claim: Ejection of the extended strand allows it to anneal with the complementary DNA on the other side of the DSB.
source: In the simplest case, ejection of this extended strand allows it to anneal with the complementary DNA on the other side of the DSB (Mehta and Haber, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mehta and Haber, 2014.

claim: RPA is a critical component of the DNA strand exchange reaction.
source: Such experiments established RPA as a critical component of the DNA strand exchange reaction (Sung, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sung, 1994.

claim: When RPA is added to the strand exchange reaction concomitantly with Rad51, the stimulatory effect of RPA is abolished.
source: However, when RPA was added to the reaction concomitantly with Rad51, which more closely reflects the situation in vivo, the stimulatory effect of RPA was abolished.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about RPA's paradoxical effect.

claim: Other proteins involved in HR serve as auxiliary factors that interact directly with Rad51 and can negate the inhibitory effect of RPA.
source: This paradoxical finding led to the discovery that other proteins known to be involved in HR serve as auxiliary factors that interact directly with Rad51 and can negate the inhibitory effect of RPA (Hays et al., 1995; Johnson and Symington, 1995; Sung, 1997a; Sung, 1997b; Tsutsui et al., 2000; Tsutsui et al., 2001; Jensen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Hays et al., 1995; Johnson and Symington, 1995; Sung, 1997a; Sung, 1997b; Tsutsui et al., 2000; Tsutsui et al., 2001; Jensen et al., 2010).

claim: Numerous distinct families of recombination auxiliary factors have been identified throughout eukaryotes, including Rad52, BRCA2, Rad54, Rad51 paralogs, Swi5-Sfr1 and the Shu complex.
source: Numerous distinct families of recombination auxiliary factors have been identified throughout eukaryotes, including Rad52, BRCA2, Rad54, Rad51 paralogs, Swi5-Sfr1 and the Shu complex (Zelensky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zelensky et al., 2014.

claim: Each group of auxiliary factors is thought to have non-overlapping roles in HR.
source: Each group is thought to have non-overlapping roles in HR, although the mechanistic differences are yet to be elucidated (Akamatsu et al., 2007; Khasanov et al., 2004; Martín et al., 2006; Shor et al., 2005; Sugawara et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Akamatsu et al., 2007; Khasanov et al., 2004; Martín et al., 2006; Shor et al., 2005; Sugawara et al., 2003).

claim: Aside from the Shu complex, all auxiliary factors are capable of binding directly to Rad51.
source: Aside from the Shu complex, all auxiliary factors are capable of binding directly to Rad51, which is thought to be essential for their respective roles in HR (Zelensky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zelensky et al., 2014.

claim: Sfr1 was first discovered in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe as an interactor of Rad51.
source: Sfr1 was first discovered in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe as an interactor of Rad51, and along with Swi5, was shown to comprise an HR sub-pathway that functions independently of and in parallel to the Rad51 paralogs Rad55-Rad57 (Akamatsu et al., 2003; Akamatsu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Akamatsu et al., 2003 and Akamatsu et al., 2007.

claim: Swi5-Sfr1 comprises an HR sub-pathway that functions independently of and in parallel to the Rad51 paralogs Rad55-Rad57.
source: Sfr1 was first discovered in the fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe as an interactor of Rad51, and along with Swi5, was shown to comprise an HR sub-pathway that functions independently of and in parallel to the Rad51 paralogs Rad55-Rad57 (Akamatsu et al., 2003; Akamatsu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Akamatsu et al., 2003 and Akamatsu et al., 2007.

claim: Substoichiometric concentrations of Swi5-Sfr1 are able to efficiently stimulate the strand exchange activity of Rad51 and Dmc1.
source: Subsequent biochemical reconstitutions demonstrated that substoichiometric concentrations of Swi5-Sfr1 were able to efficiently stimulate the strand exchange activity of Rad51 and Dmc1, the meiosis-specific RecA-family recombinase (Haruta et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haruta et al., 2006.

claim: Enhancement of strand exchange by Swi5-Sfr1 was attributed to stabilization of the nucleoprotein filaments and stimulation of the recombinases' ATPase activity.
source: This enhancement of strand exchange was attributed to stabilization of the nucleoprotein filaments and stimulation of the recombinases' ATPase activity (Haruta et al., 2006; Kurokawa et al., 2008; Murayama et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Haruta et al., 2006; Kurokawa et al., 2008; Murayama et al., 2013.

claim: Rad51-driven DNA strand exchange fits a three-step kinetic model with two reaction intermediates.
source: Rad51-driven DNA strand exchange was recently shown to fit a three-step kinetic model with two reaction intermediates (Ito et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ito et al., 2018.

claim: Swi5-Sfr1 enhanced transitioning of the first three-strand intermediate (paranemic joint) into the second three-strand intermediate (plectonemic joint).
source: Swi5-Sfr1 enhanced transitioning of the first three-strand intermediate (corresponding to a paranemic joint) into the second three-strand intermediate (corresponding to a plectonemic joint), and conversion of the second intermediate into reaction products, thus making it the only auxiliary factor known to potentiate Rad51 in both the presynaptic and synaptic phases of DNA strand exchange.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ito et al., 2018.

claim: Swi5-Sfr1 is the only auxiliary factor known to potentiate Rad51 in both the presynaptic and synaptic phases of DNA strand exchange.
source: Swi5-Sfr1 enhanced transitioning of the first three-strand intermediate (corresponding to a paranemic joint) into the second three-strand intermediate (corresponding to a plectonemic joint), and conversion of the second intermediate into reaction products, thus making it the only auxiliary factor known to potentiate Rad51 in both the presynaptic and synaptic phases of DNA strand exchange.
evidence: This is inferred from the unique properties of Swi5-Sfr1 described in the text.

claim: Limited proteolysis of Swi5-Sfr1 yielded a stable C-terminal Sfr1 fragment in complex with Swi5 (Swi5-Sfr1C, residues 181–299 of Sfr1).
source: Limited proteolysis of Swi5-Sfr1 yielded a stable C-terminal Sfr1 fragment in complex with Swi5 (Swi5-Sfr1C, residues 181–299 of Sfr1; Kuwabara et al., 2010), and this, along with the N-terminal half of Sfr1 (Sfr1N, residues 1–176 of Sfr1), could be stably expressed and purified (Kuwabara et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kuwabara et al., 2010 and Kuwabara et al., 2012.

claim: Sfr1N was predicted to be intrinsically disordered.
source: Whereas Sfr1N was predicted to be intrinsically disordered (Kokabu et al., 2011; Saikusa et al., 2013), crystallographic analyses demonstrated that Swi5-Sfr1C forms a kinked structure that is able to stimulate Rad51-driven strand exchange by stabilizing the presynaptic filament and enhancing the ATPase activity of Rad51 (Kuwabara et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kokabu et al., 2011 and Saikusa et al., 2013.

claim: Swi5-Sfr1C forms a kinked structure that is able to stimulate Rad51-driven strand exchange by stabilizing the presynaptic filament and enhancing the ATPase activity of Rad51.
source: Whereas Sfr1N was predicted to be intrinsically disordered (Kokabu et al., 2011; Saikusa et al., 2013), crystallographic analyses demonstrated that Swi5-Sfr1C forms a kinked structure that is able to stimulate Rad51-driven strand exchange by stabilizing the presynaptic filament and enhancing the ATPase activity of Rad51 (Kuwabara et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuwabara et al., 2012.

claim: Sfr1N had no direct effect on Rad51 filament stabilization or ATPase activity but was seen to co-immunoprecipitate with Rad51.
source: By contrast, Sfr1N had no direct effect on these activities but was seen to co-immunoprecipitate (co-IP) with Rad51.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuwabara et al., 2012.

claim: Complex formation between Rad51 and Swi5-Sfr1C was not detected.
source: Such complex formation was not detected between Rad51 and Swi5-Sfr1C, despite the stimulatory effect of Swi5-Sfr1C on Rad51.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuwabara et al., 2012.

claim: Swi5-Sfr1C was only able to stimulate Rad51 activity when present at much higher concentrations than full-length Swi5-Sfr1.
source: Taken together with the observation that Swi5-Sfr1C was only able to stimulate Rad51 activity when present at much higher concentrations than full-length Swi5-Sfr1, these results led to a model in which Sfr1N keeps Swi5-Sfr1C anchored in close proximity to Rad51 (Kuwabara et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuwabara et al., 2012.

claim: A model was proposed in which Sfr1N keeps Swi5-Sfr1C anchored in close proximity to Rad51.
source: Taken together with the observation that Swi5-Sfr1C was only able to stimulate Rad51 activity when present at much higher concentrations than full-length Swi5-Sfr1, these results led to a model in which Sfr1N keeps Swi5-Sfr1C anchored in close proximity to Rad51 (Kuwabara et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuwabara et al., 2012.

claim: Sfr1N did not have any stimulatory effect on DNA strand exchange even when present with Swi5-Sfr1C.
source: Even in this setting, Sfr1N did not have any stimulatory effect on DNA strand exchange (Figure 1B,C), raising the possibility that it is dispensable for the physiological function of Swi5-Sfr1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Both sfr1N and sfr1C strains showed the same sensitivity to DNA damage as the sfr1Δ strain.
source: Both strains showed the same sensitivity to DNA damage as a strain in which Sfr1 was completely absent (sfr1Δ; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Combining sfr1N or sfr1C truncations with rad55Δ sensitized cells to DNA damaging agents to the same degree as the rad55Δ sfr1Δ strain.
source: Furthermore, combining these truncations with rad55Δ sensitized cells to DNA damaging agents to the same degree as the rad55Δ sfr1Δ strain, which displays a complete loss of Rad51-dependent DNA repair (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Akamatsu et al., 2003; Akamatsu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citations to Akamatsu et al., 2003; Akamatsu et al., 2007.

claim: The rad55Δ sfr1Δ strain displays a complete loss of Rad51-dependent DNA repair.
source: Furthermore, combining these truncations with rad55Δ sensitized cells to DNA damaging agents to the same degree as the rad55Δ sfr1Δ strain, which displays a complete loss of Rad51-dependent DNA repair (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Akamatsu et al., 2003; Akamatsu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Akamatsu et al., 2003 and Akamatsu et al., 2007.

claim: Sfr1N and Sfr1C were detected at comparable levels to full-length Sfr1 by immunoblotting.
source: Sfr1N and Sfr1C were detected at comparable levels to full-length Sfr1 by immunoblotting, indicating that the sensitivity of the sfr1N and sfr1C strains is not due to a reduction in protein levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The sensitivity of the sfr1N and sfr1C strains is not due to a reduction in protein levels.
source: Sfr1N and Sfr1C were detected at comparable levels to full-length Sfr1 by immunoblotting, indicating that the sensitivity of the sfr1N and sfr1C strains is not due to a reduction in protein levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the immunoblotting data showing comparable protein levels.

claim: The sensitivity of sfr1N and sfr1C strains was not rescued by fusing Sfr1N or Sfr1C to the SV40 large T antigen nuclear localization signal.
source: Furthermore, this sensitivity was not rescued by fusing Sfr1N or Sfr1C to the SV40 large T antigen nuclear localization signal, suggesting that the observed phenotype is not caused by a failure to localize to the nucleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The observed phenotype of sfr1N and sfr1C strains is not caused by a failure to localize to the nucleus.
source: Furthermore, this sensitivity was not rescued by fusing Sfr1N or Sfr1C to the SV40 large T antigen nuclear localization signal, suggesting that the observed phenotype is not caused by a failure to localize to the nucleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of rescue by nuclear localization signal fusion.

claim: Sfr1N is essential for the function of Swi5-Sfr1 in promoting Rad51-dependent DNA repair.
source: Thus, although not essential for stimulation of Rad51 in vitro, Sfr1N is essential for the function of Swi5-Sfr1 in promoting Rad51-dependent DNA repair.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined in vitro and in vivo data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The far-UV CD spectrum of Sfr1N lacked local minima above 210 nm and showed a negative peak at ~200 nm.
source: The far-UV CD spectrum of Sfr1N lacked local minima above 210 nm and showed a negative peak at ~200 nm (Figure 2A), implying a lack of secondary structural units such as α-helices and β-sheets (Greenfield, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The CD spectrum of Sfr1N implies a lack of secondary structural units such as α-helices and β-sheets.
source: The far-UV CD spectrum of Sfr1N lacked local minima above 210 nm and showed a negative peak at ~200 nm (Figure 2A), implying a lack of secondary structural units such as α-helices and β-sheets (Greenfield, 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the CD spectrum and supported by citation to Greenfield, 2006.

claim: Most of the main chain amide protons of Sfr1N resonated in a narrow chemical shift range between 7.7 and 8.7 ppm.
source: Furthermore, examination of the 1H-15N heteronuclear single quantum coherence (HSQC) spectrum of Sfr1N revealed that most of the main chain amide protons resonated in a narrow chemical shift range between 7.7 and 8.7 ppm (Figure 2B), which is a characteristic feature of disordered proteins (Konrat, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A narrow chemical shift range between 7.7 and 8.7 ppm is a characteristic feature of disordered proteins.
source: Furthermore, examination of the 1H-15N heteronuclear single quantum coherence (HSQC) spectrum of Sfr1N revealed that most of the main chain amide protons resonated in a narrow chemical shift range between 7.7 and 8.7 ppm (Figure 2B), which is a characteristic feature of disordered proteins (Konrat, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Konrat, 2014.

claim: The majority of Sfr1N residues showed 13C secondary chemical shift values within a limited range, suggesting that random coil structures are present in these regions.
source: The majority of Sfr1N residues showed 13C secondary chemical shift values within a limited range, suggesting that random coil structures are present in these regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the secondary chemical shift analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A few groups of residues in Sfr1N exhibited more than three consecutive secondary chemical shift values outside of the random coil range, raising the possibility that some structures resembling α-helices (E27 to D29, D32 to Q34) or β-strands (L103 to K105, R161 to K164) may form within Sfr1N.
source: Nonetheless, a few groups of residues exhibited more than three consecutive secondary chemical shift values outside of this range, raising the possibility that some structures resembling α-helices (E27 to D29, D32 to Q34) or β-strands (L103 to K105, R161 to K164) may form within Sfr1N (Wishart and Sykes, 1994).
evidence: This is inferred from the secondary chemical shift analysis and supported by citation to Wishart and Sykes, 1994.

claim: TALOS+ predicted Sfr1N to be entirely disordered, with a low probability for α-helix formation from E27 to S33.
source: Further secondary structure analysis was performed using the 1HN, 13Cα, 13Cβ, 13CO, and 15NH chemical shift values and the program TALOS+ (Shen et al., 2009), which predicted Sfr1N to be entirely disordered, with a low probability for α-helix formation from E27 to S33 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and citation to Shen et al., 2009.

claim: NOE values for all residues of Sfr1N were less than 0.44, indicating that the entire protein is flexible with pico-to-nanosecond timescale motions.
source: NOE values for all residues was less than 0.44, indicating that the entire protein is flexible with pico-to-nanosecond timescale motions (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Fast motions with pico-to-nanosecond timescale are typically observed for unstructured proteins.
source: Such fast motions are typically observed for unstructured proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein dynamics.

claim: The average NOE value for all Sfr1N residues was 0.15.
source: While the average NOE values for all Sfr1N residues was 0.15, residues E27 to S33 showed slightly increased values with an average of 0.32.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Residues E27 to S33 of Sfr1N showed slightly increased NOE values with an average of 0.32.
source: While the average NOE values for all Sfr1N residues was 0.15, residues E27 to S33 showed slightly increased values with an average of 0.32.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The N-terminal half of Sfr1 is intrinsically disordered and flexible.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that, unlike the structured Swi5-Sfr1C complex (Kuwabara et al., 2012), the N-terminal half of Sfr1 is intrinsically disordered and flexible.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined CD, NMR, and NOE data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The disordered state of Sfr1N may have been conserved throughout evolution.
source: Disorder predictions using DISOPRED3 (Jones and Cozzetto, 2015) suggest that the disordered state of Sfr1N may have been conserved throughout evolution (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, see Discussion for more details).
evidence: This is inferred from disorder predictions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and supported by citation to Jones and Cozzetto, 2015.

claim: 19 out of 142 non-overlapped residues of Sfr1N showed a reduction in signal intensity of >80% upon addition of Rad51 at a 1:0.25 ratio.
source: The most prominent spectral changes, defined as a reduction in signal intensity of >80% (Sfr1N:Rad51 ratio of 1:0.25), were observed for 19 out of 142 non-overlapped residues (Figure 3B,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B,E.

claim: 18 residues of Sfr1N experienced signal intensity reductions of 60–80% upon addition of Rad51.
source: In addition to these marked changes, 18 and 20 residues experienced signal intensity reductions of 60–80% and 40–60%, respectively (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 20 residues of Sfr1N experienced signal intensity reductions of 40–60% upon addition of Rad51.
source: In addition to these marked changes, 18 and 20 residues experienced signal intensity reductions of 60–80% and 40–60%, respectively (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Five residues (A71, T73, D75, L76, and T146) of Sfr1N displayed incremental chemical shift changes and reductions in signal intensity upon addition of increasing amounts of Rad51.
source: However, five residues (A71, T73, D75, L76, and T146) displayed incremental chemical shift changes and reductions in signal intensity upon addition of increasing amounts of Rad51 (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Two sites in Sfr1N, Site 1 (S84 to T114) and Site 2 (T152 to S168), are important for the Sfr1N-Rad51 interaction.
source: These findings implicate two sites in Sfr1N, Site 1 (S84 to T114) and Site 2 (T152 to S168), where the most significantly attenuated signal intensities are sandwiched by moderately attenuated signal intensities (Figure 3E), as being important for the Sfr1N-Rad51 interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR interaction analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Site 1 of Sfr1N is highly basic and hydrophobic compared to other regions of Sfr1N.
source: Site 1 is highly basic and hydrophobic compared to other regions of Sfr1N.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Positively charged residues are a prominent feature of Site 2 of Sfr1N, but this site is not especially hydrophobic.
source: Positively charged residues are also a prominent feature of Site 2, but this site is not especially hydrophobic.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Both Sites 1 and 2 of Sfr1N are involved in electrostatic interactions with Rad51.
source: These results suggest that, while both Sites 1 and 2 are involved in electrostatic interactions with Rad51, Site 1 may also participate in hydrophobic interactions with Rad51.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence features and NMR interaction data.

claim: Site 1 of Sfr1N may also participate in hydrophobic interactions with Rad51.
source: These results suggest that, while both Sites 1 and 2 are involved in electrostatic interactions with Rad51, Site 1 may also participate in hydrophobic interactions with Rad51.
evidence: This is inferred from the hydrophobic nature of Site 1.

claim: S. pombe Rad51 exists as a multimer in solution, with a size corresponding to ~160 kDa.
source: We note that, like all RecA-family recombinases, S. pombe Rad51 exists as a multimer in solution, with a size corresponding to ~160 kDa (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, see Discussion for more details).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Several residues within Site 1 of Sfr1N showed robust crosslinking to Rad51.
source: Whereas several positions within Site 1 showed robust crosslinking to Rad51, positions within Site 2 showed little crosslinking (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), perhaps because the associations between Site 2 and Rad51 are more transient than those involving Site 1 (see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Positions within Site 2 of Sfr1N showed little crosslinking to Rad51.
source: Whereas several positions within Site 1 showed robust crosslinking to Rad51, positions within Site 2 showed little crosslinking (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), perhaps because the associations between Site 2 and Rad51 are more transient than those involving Site 1 (see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The associations between Site 2 of Sfr1N and Rad51 may be more transient than those involving Site 1.
source: Whereas several positions within Site 1 showed robust crosslinking to Rad51, positions within Site 2 showed little crosslinking (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), perhaps because the associations between Site 2 and Rad51 are more transient than those involving Site 1 (see Discussion).
evidence: This is speculated based on the differential crosslinking results.

claim: Two sites within Sfr1N, designated as Sites 1 and 2, interact with Rad51.
source: Taken together, the results obtained from the NMR interaction analysis and Site-specific crosslinking experiments indicate that two sites within Sfr1N, designated as Sites 1 and 2, interact with Rad51.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined NMR and crosslinking data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: A sequence alignment of Sfr1 orthologs within the genus Schizosaccharomyces highlighted conserved patches of positively charged residues in Sites 1 and 2.
source: A sequence alignment of Sfr1 orthologs within the genus Schizosaccharomyces highlighted conserved patches of positively charged residues in Sites 1 and 2 (bold residues in blue typeface, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Sfr1N only co-IPs with Rad51 under low-salt conditions.
source: Combined with the knowledge that Sfr1N only co-IPs with Rad51 under low-salt conditions (Kuwabara et al., 2012), it seemed plausible that these residues might be important for electrostatic interactions with Rad51.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuwabara et al., 2012.

claim: The conserved positively charged residues in Sites 1 and 2 of Sfr1N might be important for electrostatic interactions with Rad51.
source: Combined with the knowledge that Sfr1N only co-IPs with Rad51 under low-salt conditions (Kuwabara et al., 2012), it seemed plausible that these residues might be important for electrostatic interactions with Rad51.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence conservation and salt-sensitivity of the interaction.

claim: A substantial fraction of wild-type Swi5-Sfr1 was recovered in the Rad51-bound fraction in the Affi-gel interaction assay.
source: A substantial fraction of wild-type Swi5-Sfr1 was recovered in the eluate (Rad51-bound fraction), although some of the protein remained in the flow-through (unbound fraction; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The amount of 3A and 4A mutant proteins detected in the Rad51-bound fraction was reduced compared to wild-type.
source: By contrast, the amount of 3A and 4A mutant proteins detected in the eluate was reduced, with much of the protein remaining in the flow-through.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The 7A mutant protein was barely detected in the Rad51-bound fraction.
source: The 7A mutant protein was barely detected in the eluate, indicating that the binding seen in the 3A mutant was dependent on Site 2 and the binding seen in the 4A mutant was dependent on Site 1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The binding seen in the 3A mutant was dependent on Site 2.
source: The 7A mutant protein was barely detected in the eluate, indicating that the binding seen in the 3A mutant was dependent on Site 2 and the binding seen in the 4A mutant was dependent on Site 1.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of 3A and 7A mutants.

claim: The binding seen in the 4A mutant was dependent on Site 1.
source: The 7A mutant protein was barely detected in the eluate, indicating that the binding seen in the 3A mutant was dependent on Site 2 and the binding seen in the 4A mutant was dependent on Site 1.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of 4A and 7A mutants.

claim: Sites 1 and 2 facilitate the binding of Swi5-Sfr1 to Rad51 in a cooperative manner.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Sites 1 and 2 facilitate the binding of Swi5-Sfr1 to Rad51 in a cooperative manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined pull-down and co-IP data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Substoichiometric concentrations of the 7A mutant failed to efficiently stimulate Rad51-driven strand exchange.
source: Consistent with the observed binding defect, substoichiometric concentrations of the 7A mutant failed to efficiently stimulate Rad51-driven strand exchange, with a higher concentration of mutant protein required to achieve a wild-type level of joint molecules (JM, reaction intermediates) and nicked-circles (NCs, reaction products; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: At 0.25 µM, the defect of the 7A protein was more pronounced for NC (~15 fold reduction) than JM (~5 fold reduction).
source: At 0.25 µM, the defect of the 7A protein was more pronounced for NC (~15 fold reduction) than JM (~5 fold reduction), suggesting that the ability of Swi5-Sfr1 to stimulate both the initial pairing of homologous DNA and the subsequent strand transfer by Rad51 are defective when the interaction with Sites 1 and 2 is ablated (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D–F.

claim: The ability of Swi5-Sfr1 to stimulate both the initial pairing of homologous DNA and the subsequent strand transfer by Rad51 are defective when the interaction with Sites 1 and 2 is ablated.
source: At 0.25 µM, the defect of the 7A protein was more pronounced for NC (~15 fold reduction) than JM (~5 fold reduction), suggesting that the ability of Swi5-Sfr1 to stimulate both the initial pairing of homologous DNA and the subsequent strand transfer by Rad51 are defective when the interaction with Sites 1 and 2 is ablated (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on JM and NC formation.

claim: The 3A and 4A mutants were able to promote efficient JM and NC formation at substoichiometric concentrations.
source: By contrast, the 3A and 4A mutants were able to promote efficient JM and NC formation at substoichiometric concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The loss of Rad51 stimulation observed at higher concentrations of wild-type Swi5-Sfr1 was attenuated in the 3A and 4A mutants.
source: Nevertheless, the loss of Rad51 stimulation observed at higher concentrations of wild-type Swi5-Sfr1 was attenuated in the 3A and 4A mutants (Figure 5C lanes 6, 21 and 28), suggesting that this loss of stimulation occurs due to unproductive interactions with Rad51 or sequestration of DNA substrates by Swi5-Sfr1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The loss of stimulation at high Swi5-Sfr1 concentrations occurs due to unproductive interactions with Rad51 or sequestration of DNA substrates by Swi5-Sfr1.
source: Nevertheless, the loss of Rad51 stimulation observed at higher concentrations of wild-type Swi5-Sfr1 was attenuated in the 3A and 4A mutants (Figure 5C lanes 6, 21 and 28), suggesting that this loss of stimulation occurs due to unproductive interactions with Rad51 or sequestration of DNA substrates by Swi5-Sfr1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and see Discussion).
evidence: This is inferred from the behavior of the mutants and DNA binding data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Efficient stimulation of Rad51 was maintained at higher concentrations of the 7A mutant.
source: Consistent with this notion, efficient stimulation of Rad51 was maintained at higher concentrations of the 7A mutant (Figure 5C lanes 8 and 15) and Swi5-Sfr1C (Figure 1B,C; Kuwabara et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Interactions between Rad51 and both Sites 1 and 2 are important for efficient stimulation of strand exchange.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that interactions between Rad51 and both Sites 1 and 2 are important for efficient stimulation of strand exchange.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined strand exchange data for all mutants shown in Figure 5.

claim: At substoichiometric concentrations, Swi5-Sfr1 effectively stabilizes Rad51 presynaptic filaments.
source: At substoichiometric concentrations, Swi5-Sfr1 effectively stabilizes Rad51 presynaptic filaments (Kurokawa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kurokawa et al., 2008.

claim: Inclusion of wild-type Swi5-Sfr1 resulted in a slower reduction in anisotropy, indicating that Rad51 filaments had been stabilized.
source: Inclusion of wild-type Swi5-Sfr1 resulted in a slower reduction in anisotropy, indicating that Rad51 filaments had been stabilized (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Inclusion of the 7A mutant did not result in any obvious filament stabilization.
source: Strikingly, inclusion of the 7A mutant did not result in any obvious filament stabilization (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Both 3A and 4A mutants showed some stabilization of Rad51 filaments, but the magnitude of this stabilization was less than that observed for wild-type protein.
source: Furthermore, although both 3A and 4A mutants showed some stabilization of Rad51 filaments, the magnitude of this stabilization was less than that observed for wild-type protein (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: The reaction rate constants for dissociation of Rad51-ssDNA complexes (koff) showed a substantial decline in the presence of Swi5-Sfr1.
source: Consistent with these observations, the reaction rate constants for dissociation of Rad51-ssDNA complexes (koff) showed a substantial decline in the presence of Swi5-Sfr1, a lesser decline for the 3A and 4A mutants, and only a marginal decline for the 7A mutant (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Sites 1 and 2 within Sfr1N interact cooperatively with Rad51 to facilitate filament stabilization by Swi5-Sfr1.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that Sites 1 and 2 within Sfr1N interact cooperatively with Rad51 to facilitate filament stabilization by Swi5-Sfr1.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined filament stability data shown in Figure 6B-F.

claim: Swi5-Sfr1 has been shown to stimulate the ATPase activity of Rad51, which is important for efficient strand exchange.
source: In addition to stabilizing Rad51 filaments, Swi5-Sfr1 has been shown to stimulate the ATPase activity of Rad51, which is also important for efficient strand exchange (Haruta et al., 2006; Kurokawa et al., 2008; Ito et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Haruta et al., 2006; Kurokawa et al., 2008; Ito et al., 2018.

claim: Substoichiometric concentrations of Swi5-Sfr1C failed to efficiently stimulate the ATPase activity of Rad51.
source: Since substoichiometric concentrations of Swi5-Sfr1C failed to efficiently stimulate the ATPase activity of Rad51 (Kuwabara et al., 2012), we sought to determine whether Rad51-dependent ATP hydrolysis was potentiated by the 7A mutant.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kuwabara et al., 2012.

claim: Wild-type Swi5-Sfr1 was able to efficiently enhance ATP hydrolysis by Rad51 at substoichiometric concentrations (Swi5-Sfr1:Rad51 ratio of 1:20), with a 1.85-fold increase in ATP turnover.
source: As expected, wild-type Swi5-Sfr1 was able to efficiently enhance ATP hydrolysis by Rad51 at substoichiometric concentrations (Swi5-Sfr1:Rad51 ratio of 1:20), with a 1.85-fold increase in ATP turnover (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The 7A mutant only managed to enhance the ATPase activity of Rad51 1.28-fold, which is similar to the 1.27-fold stimulation observed with Swi5-Sfr1C.
source: By contrast, the 7A mutant only managed to enhance the ATPase activity of Rad51 1.28-fold, which is similar to the 1.27-fold stimulation observed with Swi5-Sfr1C.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The 3A and 4A mutants stimulated ATP hydrolysis like wild type.
source: The 3A and 4A mutants stimulated ATP hydrolysis like wild type.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Interaction of either Site 1 or 2 with Rad51 is sufficient to promote efficient stimulation of ATP hydrolysis.
source: These results suggest that interaction of either Site 1 or 2 with Rad51 is sufficient to promote efficient stimulation of ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the ATPase data for the 3A and 4A mutants.

claim: The interaction mutants did not show any obvious sensitivity to DNA damage.
source: Unexpectedly, the interaction mutants did not show any obvious sensitivity to DNA damage (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), which is in sharp contrast to the DNA repair defect of the N-terminal deletion strain (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A marginal sensitivity was observed for the sfr1-7A strain but this was not statistically significant.
source: A marginal sensitivity was observed for the sfr1-7A strain but this was not statistically significant (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In the absence of Rad55, the sfr1-7A mutant showed the same DNA damage sensitivity as the sfr1Δ mutant.
source: Strikingly, in the absence of Rad55, the sfr1-7A mutant showed the same DNA damage sensitivity as the sfr1Δ mutant (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Both the sfr1-3A and sfr1-4A mutants were more sensitive to DNA damage than sfr1+ in the rad55Δ background, although this sensitivity was not as severe as that observed for the rad55Δ sfr1Δ and rad55Δ sfr1-7A strains.
source: Furthermore, both the sfr1-3A and sfr1-4A mutants were more sensitive to DNA damage than sfr1+ in the rad55Δ background, although this sensitivity was not as severe as that observed for the rad55Δ sfr1Δ and rad55Δ sfr1-7A strains (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: Similar results to those in the rad55Δ background were obtained in the rad57Δ background.
source: Similar results were obtained in the rad57Δ background (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The residues mutated in sfr1-7A are important for DNA repair.
source: These results indicate that the residues mutated in sfr1-7A are indeed important for DNA repair, while also suggesting that the DNA repair defects of Sfr1 amino acid-substitution mutants are suppressed by a Rad55-Rad57-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic data showing DNA damage sensitivity in the rad55Δ background.

claim: The DNA repair defects of Sfr1 amino acid-substitution mutants are suppressed by a Rad55-Rad57-dependent mechanism.
source: These results indicate that the residues mutated in sfr1-7A are indeed important for DNA repair, while also suggesting that the DNA repair defects of Sfr1 amino acid-substitution mutants are suppressed by a Rad55-Rad57-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic data showing DNA damage sensitivity only in the rad55Δ background.

claim: An interaction between Rad57 and Rad51 has been reported by yeast two-hybrid analysis.
source: While an interaction between Rad57 and Rad51 has been reported by yeast two-hybrid analysis (Tsutsui et al., 2001), a possible interaction between Rad55-Rad57 and Swi5-Sfr1 was never examined due to the genetic evidence suggesting that they comprise independent sub-pathways of HR (Akamatsu et al., 2003; Akamatsu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tsutsui et al., 2001.

claim: A possible interaction between Rad55-Rad57 and Swi5-Sfr1 was never examined due to genetic evidence suggesting that they comprise independent sub-pathways of HR.
source: While an interaction between Rad57 and Rad51 has been reported by yeast two-hybrid analysis (Tsutsui et al., 2001), a possible interaction between Rad55-Rad57 and Swi5-Sfr1 was never examined due to the genetic evidence suggesting that they comprise independent sub-pathways of HR (Akamatsu et al., 2003; Akamatsu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Akamatsu et al., 2003 and Akamatsu et al., 2007.

claim: Rad55 and Rad57 were present in seemingly stoichiometric amounts in the partially purified protein preparation.
source: Rad55 and Rad57 constituted the two major bands in this partially purified protein preparation and were present in seemingly stoichiometric amounts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), consistent with previous reports in budding yeast (Sung, 1997a; Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and citations to Sung, 1997a and Liu et al., 2011.

claim: Rad55 co-IP'd with Rad57.
source: As expected, Rad55 was found to co-IP with Rad57 (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Both Swi5-Sfr1 and Swi5-Sfr1-7A co-IP'd with Rad57.
source: Moreover, both Swi5-Sfr1 and Swi5-Sfr1-7A coIP'd with Rad57.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Rad51 was completely undetectable in the anti-Rad57 immunoprecipitates.
source: Importantly, Rad51 was completely undetectable in these immunoprecipitates (Figure 7F), suggesting that Swi5-Sfr1 and Rad55-Rad57 directly interact in a Rad51-independent manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Swi5-Sfr1 and Rad55-Rad57 directly interact in a Rad51-independent manner.
source: Importantly, Rad51 was completely undetectable in these immunoprecipitates (Figure 7F), suggesting that Swi5-Sfr1 and Rad55-Rad57 directly interact in a Rad51-independent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of Rad51 in the Rad57 immunoprecipitates containing Swi5-Sfr1.

claim: The N-terminal half of Sfr1 was found to be essential for the role of Swi5-Sfr1 in promoting Rad51-dependent DNA repair.
source: In this study, we characterized the interaction between Rad51, the key protein in HR, and Swi5-Sfr1, a widely conserved recombination auxiliary factor. The N-terminal half of Sfr1 was found to be essential for the role of Swi5-Sfr1 in promoting Rad51-dependent DNA repair (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: The N-terminal domain of Sfr1 was shown to be intrinsically disordered.
source: This domain was shown to be intrinsically disordered (Figure 2) and contain two sites that interact with Rad51 (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Mutation of the two interaction sites in Sfr1N disrupted the physical and functional interaction with Rad51 in vitro.
source: Although mutation of the two interaction sites disrupted the physical and functional interaction with Rad51 in vitro (Figures 5 and 6), unexpectedly, defects in DNA repair were only observed in the absence of Rad55-Rad57, another auxiliary factor complex with which Swi5-Sfr1 was found to interact (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Defects in DNA repair for the Sfr1N interaction mutants were only observed in the absence of Rad55-Rad57.
source: Although mutation of the two interaction sites disrupted the physical and functional interaction with Rad51 in vitro (Figures 5 and 6), unexpectedly, defects in DNA repair were only observed in the absence of Rad55-Rad57, another auxiliary factor complex with which Swi5-Sfr1 was found to interact (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: Swi5-Sfr1 was found to interact with Rad55-Rad57.
source: Although mutation of the two interaction sites disrupted the physical and functional interaction with Rad51 in vitro (Figures 5 and 6), unexpectedly, defects in DNA repair were only observed in the absence of Rad55-Rad57, another auxiliary factor complex with which Swi5-Sfr1 was found to interact (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figure 7E,F.
